newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL stock market ignores Singapore-Malaysia row.
newsitem.headline: KL stock market ignores Singapore-Malaysia row.

text.p: The war of words between Singapore and Malaysia over remarks made by Singapore's Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew was largely ignored at Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange on Thursday, analysts and dealers said.
They said the market was not unduly worried unless the row went beyond words and was not soon resolved.
But they added that a prolonged row could hurt stocks of property companies in Johor which has a large exposure to Singapore property buyers.
"I really don't think it's an issue," said Simon Maughan, head of research at brokers W.I. Carr in Kuala Lumpur.
"The stock market does not really react to the squabbles between Malaysia and Singapore," he added.

Malaysian newspapers on Wednesday reported Lee Kuan Yew's description of Johor state as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" in an affidavit filed in a Singapore court on January 27 in relation to libel action against an opposition politician.
Malaysia has asked for retraction and apology of Lee's comments, and the news was a factor in the weakness of Singapore shares on Thursday.
Trading on the exchange has been heavy in recent weeks, dominated by retail players chasing up prices of the smaller-capitalised stocks.
But several Malaysian listed companies which derive considerable amounts of their income from property development projects in Johor could be affected if the worries continue.
An example is infrastructure conglomerate Renong Bhd which is building a large township in Johor and a second causeway linking Malaysia and Singapore.

"If there's any impact at all (from the squabble), it could be on companies like Kemayan, Pelangi, Bandar Raya, Pembinaan Setia, Renong and United Engineers," said Faez Khairuddin, head of research at S.J. Securities.
In early afternoon trading, the stocks were flat to slightly lower to reflect the soft tone of the broader market.

"These are all property development companies with considerable exposure to the Singapore market," said Faez, referring to Singaporeans who invest in property in Johor due to the considerably lower land costs compared to their own country.
